agentmemory.q: Why does a chatbot seem to remember earlier messages in the same conversation?
options: The model stores each user's messages inside its weights
The application sends the earlier messages again with each call
The provider keeps a private copy of every chat for the model
The model caches answers and replays them
agentmemory.why: Models are stateless. The app re-sends the thread each turn; nothing is learned into the weights during a chat.

agentmemory.q: Which is an example of episodic memory?
options: The customer prefers replies in German
Always check the staging database before production
On 3 March the export job failed with a timeout
The account is on the Pro plan
agentmemory.why: Episodic memory stores dated events and outcomes. A preference or plan is semantic; a 'how to' rule is procedural.

agentmemory.q: A support agent's thread keeps overflowing after big tool results. What is the best first change?
options: Switch to a model with a larger window and change nothing else
Save every tool result to long-term memory instead
Compact at about 80 percent: summarise old turns and replace bulky tool results with short notes
Ask users to keep their messages shorter
agentmemory.why: Compacting before the limit, and trimming bulky tool output, keeps room for the next turn. A bigger window only delays the problem and raises cost.

agentmemory.q: Halden's security team asks how one handler team is kept from seeing another team's memories. Best answer?
options: The system prompt tells the model not to reveal other teams' data
Every memory row has tenant and team ids, and one data-access function filters on them
Memories are encrypted, so leaks are harmless
We trust that handlers only ask about their own claims
agentmemory.why: Isolation must be enforced in code or the database. A prompt instruction can be ignored or bypassed by injection.

agentmemory.q: Spot the mistake: 'Our agent saves every sentence the user types as a long-term fact, so it never forgets anything.'
options: Nothing, saving everything is the safest design
It saves guesses, stale values and injected instructions, which later come back as false facts
The only problem is storage cost
It should save only the assistant's replies instead
agentmemory.why: Without a write policy, memory fills with noise and even prompt-injected rules. Storage cost is the smaller problem.

llmobs.q: In LLM tracing, what is a span?
options: One timed step inside a request, such as a model or tool call
The full history of one user across all their sessions
A daily summary of token usage per customer
The time window used to sample traces for evals
llmobs.why: A trace is one request; spans are its timed steps, nested in a tree. Session history and daily summaries are different things.

llmobs.q: Why use OpenTelemetry's GenAI attribute names such as gen_ai.usage.input_tokens?
options: They make model calls cheaper
They are required by law for AI systems
Tools and backends can read your spans the same way, so you can switch vendors
They automatically redact personal data
llmobs.why: Semantic conventions are shared names, so any compatible backend understands your data. They do not cut cost or redact anything.

llmobs.q: A customer says the assistant got slower this week. What do you look at first?
options: The monthly invoice from the model provider
p50 and p95 latency per span type this week versus last week
A new, faster model to try in production
The number of thumbs-up clicks
llmobs.why: Per-span latency percentiles show which step got slower. Swapping models before knowing the cause is guessing.

llmobs.q: A bank's privacy officer asks what your traces contain. Which plan is best?
options: Store full prompts forever in a third-party tool, since debugging needs them
Store no traces at all, to be safe
Redact PII before export, store in an approved region, limit access and set retention
Encrypt traces and skip the retention question
llmobs.why: Redaction before export, approved location, access control and retention together answer the question. No traces at all leaves you blind.

llmobs.q: Spot the mistake: 'We collect thumbs-down clicks in a table. Quality will improve over time.'
options: Thumbs-down data is useless and should not be collected
Clicks need a trace id, regular review, root-cause labels and new eval cases to change anything
They should collect only thumbs-up clicks
Nothing, collecting feedback is enough
llmobs.why: Unreviewed feedback changes nothing. Linking it to traces and turning failures into eval cases closes the loop.

labeling.q: What does Cohen's kappa add that percent agreement does not?
options: It counts how many items each annotator labeled
It corrects for agreement that would happen by chance
It measures how accurate the model is on the labels
It weights each label by how costly a mistake is
labeling.why: Kappa compares observed agreement with the agreement expected from each person's label mix, so common labels do not inflate the score.

labeling.q: What is a gold question in a labeling project?
options: The hardest item in the batch, sent to the customer
A question the annotators ask the adjudicator
An item with a known answer hidden in normal work to check accuracy
The first item labeled, used as a style example
labeling.why: Gold questions have trusted answers and are mixed in secretly, so you can score each annotator over time and catch drift.

labeling.q: Two annotators disagree on 30 percent of a customer's documents. What do you do first?
options: Replace them with a more experienced pair
Average their labels and move on
Train the model anyway, since it will learn the majority
Read the disagreements to find unclear or missing guideline rules
labeling.why: Most disagreement comes from unclear rules. Reading the disputed items shows which rule to add or fix; new people with the same guideline would disagree too.

labeling.q: A retailer has 40,000 unlabeled tickets and budget for 1,000 labels. Which choice uses the budget best?
options: Label the tickets the current model is least sure about, plus some random ones
Label the 1,000 newest tickets only
Label the tickets the model is most confident about
Label only tickets longer than 200 words
labeling.why: This is active learning: uncertain items teach the model most, and a random share keeps the batch from filling with duplicates or junk.

labeling.q: Spot the mistake: 'Our two labelers agree 92 percent, so the labels are reliable.' 90 percent of items are 'no issue'.
options: Nothing is wrong; 92 percent is above any reasonable bar
With one label at 90 percent, chance alone gives high agreement; check kappa and per-label counts
Agreement should be measured by the model, not by people
They should have used three labelers, so 92 percent is meaningless
labeling.why: When one label dominates, people agree often by luck. Kappa and per-label agreement show whether they agree on the rare labels that matter.

voice.q: What is barge-in in a voice agent?
options: The agent calling a customer back after a dropped call
The caller speaking while the agent talks, so the agent should stop and listen
A supervisor joining a live call to listen
The agent transferring the call to a human
voice.why: Barge-in is the caller interrupting. The agent should stop its audio quickly, clear queued audio and record only what the caller heard.

voice.q: Why do voice agents usually receive phone audio over a WebSocket?
options: It compresses audio better than any other method
Phone networks only support WebSockets
It keeps a two-way connection open, so audio frames flow both ways during the call
It encrypts the audio so no consent is needed
voice.why: A WebSocket stays open so small audio frames can stream in and out continuously. It does not remove consent rules or compress audio by itself.

voice.q: A voice agent keeps cutting callers off while they read their account number. What do you change first?
options: Lengthen the end-of-turn wait after the agent asks for a number
Switch to a larger LLM
Turn off barge-in completely
Ask callers to speak faster
voice.why: People pause between digit groups. A context-dependent endpointing wait fixes it without slowing every other turn.

voice.q: Turns take 2 seconds. Logs show TTS starts only after the full LLM reply. Best fix?
options: Buy a faster phone line
Add a filler phrase before every reply
Shorten the greeting
Stream the LLM output and start TTS on the first complete sentence
voice.why: Waiting for the whole reply adds the full generation time to every turn. Streaming the first sentence to TTS removes most of it.

voice.q: Spot the mistake: 'We record every call and transcript forever; callers pay by reading their card number to the agent.'
options: Nothing, recordings help debugging
Only the transcript is a problem, recordings are fine
Card numbers must stay out of recordings, and consent and retention rules must be settled
The only issue is storage cost
voice.why: Card data in recordings breaks payment security rules, and recording needs consent and a retention limit agreed with legal.
